citations.quote:
For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N,m_N)$ be a sigma-finite phase-reference measure
space from [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]; the cotangent construction uses
the stated Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]). A **statistical state** is a probability measure
$P$ on $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)$, meaning a countably additive measure with
$P(\Gamma_N)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). A **density** of $P$ relative to $m_N$ is a
measurable $\rho:\Gamma_N\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$P(A)=\int_A\rho\,dm_N\quad(A\in\mathcal F_N),\qquad \int_{\Gamma_N}\rho\,dm_N=1.$$
Equivalently, $P=\rho\,m_N$ in the definition of a measure with density
([[def-measure-with-density]]); integration against that density has the
meaning supplied by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]. A state need not
have a density.

An **observable** is a real-valued measurable function
$A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]).
Its expectation $\langle A\rangle_P:=\int A\,dP$ is used only when $A$ is
integrable, that is, $\int|A|\,dP<\infty$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). Its
variance is
$$\operatorname{Var}_P(A):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)^2\,dP$$
when $A^2$ is integrable. For square-integrable $A,B$, their covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_P(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)(B-\langle B\rangle_P)\,dP.$$
These expressions are finite under the stated square-integrability
hypotheses. Indeed, $P(\Gamma_N)=1$ makes $1\in L^2(P)$ with norm $1$.
By [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
$\int|A|\,dP\le(\int A^2\,dP)^{1/2}$, so the mean of a square-integrable
observable exists. If $a=\langle A\rangle_P$, then
$|A-a|^2\le2A^2+2a^2$ makes $A-a$ square-integrable; the same argument
applies to $B-b$. A second application of that inequality gives
$\int|(A-a)(B-b)|\,dP\le\|A-a\|_2\|B-b\|_2<\infty$.
Thus both the variance and covariance integrals above are well-defined.

If $P=\rho m_N$ and the integrals are defined, these expectations equal
$\int A\rho\,dm_N$ by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]].

A **macrostate map** is a measurable map
$M:(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)\to(Y,\mathcal G)$. Its induced state on $Y$ is
the pushforward $M_*P(B):=P(M^{-1}(B))$. The measure of a macrocell and an
entropy assigned to that macrostate are additional constructions; they are
not identical to the expectation or variance of a microscopic observable.

derivations.claim: For $x>0$, set $h(x)=x-1-\log x$. By [F1], $h'(x)=1-1/x$, which is negative for $0<x<1$ and positive for $x>1$; hence $h(x)\ge h(1)=0$, with equality only at $x=1$. On $\{p>0\}$ put $x=q/p$ to obtain $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. The negative part of the left integrand is integrable: where $q>p$, writing $x=q/p>1$ gives $p\log(q/p)=q(\log x)/x\le q$, since $h(x)\ge0$ implies $\log x\le x-1$ and $(x-1)/x\le1$. Therefore its integral is well-defined as an extended real number, and $$D(p\Vert q)\ge\int_{\{p>0\}}(p-q)\,dm =1-\int_{\{p>0\}}q\,dm\ge0.$$

If $D=0$, both nonnegative gaps in the last inequalities vanish: $q$ has no mass on $\{p=0\}$, and $h(q/p)=0$ $p$-almost everywhere. The strict equality case in step 1.1 gives $q=p$ on $\{p>0\}$, hence $p=q$ almost everywhere. Conversely, if $p=q$ almost everywhere then the defining integrand is zero and $D=0$.

In the Gibbs case, [F2] and [A2] give $\log q=-\beta H-\log Z$ $p$-almost everywhere, so all terms below are integrable and $$D(p\Vert q)=\int p\log p\,dm+\beta\langle H\rangle_p+\log Z =\beta\left(\langle H\rangle_p+\beta^{-1}\int p\log p\,dm-F\right).$$ Since $S[p]=-k\int p\log p\,dm$ and $\beta^{-1}=kT$, the middle term is $-TS[p]$. Nonnegativity and the equality condition follow from steps 1.1 and 2.1.

If a density gives positive mass to $\{q=0\}$, its extended $D$ is $+\infty$ by definition; otherwise step 1.1 applies after removal of null sets. Thus $\mathcal F_{\rm ext}\ge F$ for every probability density. The density $q$ is allowed here without any energy or entropy integrability assumption: directly $D(q\Vert q)=0$, so $\mathcal F_{\rm ext}[q]=F$. Step 2.1 gives uniqueness. Step 3.1 proves agreement with the original finite formula on $\mathcal A$, without assigning any meaning to an undefined difference $+\infty-\infty$.

Let $Q(B):=\int_Bq\,dm$. Positive finite $Z$ implies $H$ is finite $Q$-almost everywhere: $H=+\infty$ has zero Gibbs weight, while $H=-\infty$ can occur only on an $m$-null set, since its exponential weight is infinite. Set $A_n:=\{|H|\le n\}$ and $c_n:=Q(A_n)$. Then $c_n\uparrow1$. Indeed the disjoint sets $A_1,A_2\setminus A_1,\ldots$ cover the finite-energy set, so countable additivity of the probability measure $Q$ makes their partial sums $c_n$ converge to $1$. For every sufficiently large $n$, $c_n>0$ and $p_n:=q\mathbf1_{A_n}/c_n$ is a probability density. On its support $|H|\le n$ and $\log p_n=-\beta H-\log Z-\log c_n$ is bounded, so $p_n\in\mathcal A$. Moreover $p_n/q=1/c_n$ on that support, hence $$D(p_n\Vert q)=-\log c_n\longrightarrow0.$$ The limit follows from the continuity of the logarithm at $1$ supplied by [F1]. Step 3.1 now gives finite free energies $F-\beta^{-1}\log c_n\to F$, proving the stated infimum. Equality for any $p\in\mathcal A$ forces $p=q$ almost everywhere by step 2.1; consequently it is attained exactly when $q\in\mathcal A$, which is precisely the two stated integrability conditions.

Statement; proof step 5.1: H=+infinity has zero Gibbs mass and H=-infinity occurs only on an m-null set under finite Z. Finite-energy truncations have c_n increasing to one; terms on zero-density sets have the stated zero convention.

boundaries.evidence: Statement; proof steps 2.1 and 5.1: zero D forces p=q almost everywhere, so attainment in the finite class implies q has both finite integrability conditions.
Statement; proof steps 2.1 and 5.1: if q has finite energy and absolute entropy then q belongs to the finite class and its zero D attains F.

risk_review.notes: Cycle 1 owner review of every current proof step and full declared source interfaces. Steps 1.1–2.1 retain the valid negative-part estimate and both equality directions. Step 3.1 retains the finite identity with explicitly finite energy and absolute entropy; F1 supplies log laws by the displayed derivative argument. Step 4.1 defines, rather than falsely identifies, extended relative free energy when separate integrals are undefined; q is always allowed and uniquely minimizes it. Step 5.1 proves q is finite-energy almost surely, c_n rises to one by countable additivity, normalized energy truncations have finite energy and bounded log density, and D=-log c_n tends to zero. Hence the original finite class has infimum F, attained exactly iff q has the two stated integrability properties. Native heavy-tail counterexample independently confirmed by t=log x: q dm=dt/t^2 on (1,infinity), H=t+2log t, so q energy and absolute entropy diverge; truncation D tends to zero without a finite-class minimizer. Both actual direct consumers were read in full: finite mixing has Gaussian finite moments/bounded positional factors; ensemble potentials assumes finite Gibbs energy and entropy explicitly. They use the preserved identity/equality case, not a false unrestricted finite-functional minimizer. Old709/current712 dependency, discharge and body-link closure has no further item consumers.

citations.quote:
For a declared classical model with $N_a$ operationally indistinguishable
particles of each species $a$, label those particles by
$\{(a,i):1\le i\le N_a\}$ on the auxiliary labelled cover, and let
$S_{N_a}$ denote the permutation group of that species' finite label set.
The product group $G=\prod_a S_{N_a}$ acts on the labelled phase space
$\Gamma_N=T^*Q_N$ by the cotangent lifts of within-species permutations. Let
$\Pi_N:\Gamma_N\to\Gamma_N/G$ be its measurable orbit map from
[[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]. Choose $a_0>0$ as a fixed primitive
reference parameter with action units J s; [[def-cm01-units]] supplies its
dimension, not its value or the choice of this parameter. Here $d$ is the
number of spatial dimensions and $N=\sum_aN_a$. No numerical value or
identification of $a_0$ with Planck's constant is imposed.

Use the weighted labelled lift
$$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,d\Lambda_N =\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,dq\,dp$$
on $\Gamma_N$, where $d\Lambda_N$ is the Liouville density and the last
expression is its coordinate density in canonical charts, with coordinates
read in SI numerical units. The coordinate volume $dq\,dp$ has action
dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the reference is dimensionless. The
physical quotient reference is
$$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(B):=m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(\Pi_N^{-1}(B))\qquad(B\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{quot}}).$$
Thus $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on the labelled cover $\Gamma_N$, and
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}=(\Pi_N)_*m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on
$\Gamma_N/G$; with $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, the latter is exactly the normalized
quotient reference of [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]].

Physical observables for indistinguishable particles are measurable
$G$-invariant functions $A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$, equivalently measurable
functions $\bar A$ on the quotient with $A=\bar A\circ\Pi_N$. For every such
observable with an integrable expectation, its integral against
$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ equals the quotient integral against
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$. A labelled density represents a physical state on
the quotient only if it is invariant under $G$ almost everywhere with respect
to $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$; an invariant representative may then be used. In
particular, an indistinguishable-particle Hamiltonian must be invariant under
these permutations (or agree almost everywhere with its permuted versions
when only its Gibbs density is at issue). A label-specific coordinate
statistic on the lift is not itself a quotient observable. Under a
permutation-invariant state its marginal law
can instead be interpreted as the law of a uniformly selected particle within
the same species, or of a uniformly selected coordinate of the same type
within that species. Symmetric sums and averages within each species are
quotient observables.
Calculations of labelled momentum components in
[[pthm-csm-canonical-momentum-equipartition]] use this symmetric labelled
lift, and their permutation-invariant kinetic sums and averages are physical
observables.

If labels are operationally distinguishable, omit the corresponding
permutation factor and use the labelled phase space directly. The convention
is part of the preparation and reference model; it is not deduced from
Hamiltonian mechanics. Whether a quantity is represented by a gauge-dependent
canonical momentum or by a gauge-invariant mechanical momentum is fixed by the
stated model and gauge convention. No quantum exchange law, actual preparation
mechanism, or empirical indistinguishability test is asserted.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a measure space and let $p,q$ be probability
densities relative to $m$, with $q>0$ almost everywhere on $\{p>0\}$. Define
the relative entropy
$$D(p\Vert q):=\int_{\{p>0\}}p\log(p/q)\,dm,$$
allowing $+\infty$. Then $D(p\Vert q)\ge0$, and equality holds exactly
when $p=q$ almost everywhere. For arbitrary probability densities, extend
$D(p\Vert q)$ to $+\infty$ if $\int_{\{q=0\}}p\,dm>0$.
In particular, let $H$ be extended-real measurable, finite $p$-almost
everywhere, let $\beta>0$, and suppose
$$0<Z=\int e^{-\beta H}dm<\infty,\quad q=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H},\quad \int p|H|dm<\infty,\quad \int|p\log p|dm<\infty.$$
For $S[p]:=-k\int p\log p\,dm$ and $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, with $k>0$
and $\beta kT=1$, one has
$$D(p\Vert q)=\beta\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-F-TS[p]\bigr)\ge0.$$
Write $\mathcal A$ for the probability densities satisfying these finite
energy and absolute entropy conditions. For every measurable $H$ with the
stated positive finite $Z$, define the **extended relative free energy** on
all probability densities by
$$\mathcal F_{\rm ext}[p]:=F+\beta^{-1}D(p\Vert q)\in[F,+\infty].$$
It agrees with $\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]$ on $\mathcal A$ and has the
unique minimizer $q$, up to almost-everywhere equality, even when the
separate energy and entropy integrals of $q$ are not finite. Moreover,
$$\inf_{p\in\mathcal A}\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]\bigr)=F.$$
This infimum is attained if and only if
$\int q|H|dm<\infty$ and $\int|q\log q|dm<\infty$; in that case its
unique minimizer is $q$. Otherwise no density in $\mathcal A$ attains the
infimum. Products with a zero density are taken as zero on the forbidden
set, and densities may be redefined on null sets. These mathematical
claims do not derive a physical preparation.

derivations.claim: For $r$ particles in position volume $W$, separate the $r$ position integrals and use [F1] in all $dr$ momentum coordinates. For one coordinate put $a=\beta/(2m)$; integrating $\frac{d}{dp}(pe^{-ap^2})=e^{-ap^2}-2ap^2e^{-ap^2}$ over $\mathbb R$ gives $\langle p^2\rangle=m/\beta$, as the boundary term vanishes by Gaussian decay. Thus the mean kinetic energy is $dr/(2\beta)$. The position law factorizes into $r$ uniform position laws. With $\lambda_T=a_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$, the partition function is $$Z_r(W)=\frac{W^r}{r!a_0^{dr}}\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{dr/2} =\frac{(W/\lambda_T^d)^r}{r!}.$$ For equal total particle count $2N$ before and after, the $\beta U$ terms in [F2] cancel, so the entropy change is $k_B$ times the logarithm of the partition-function ratio.

Initially the ratio is $Z_{2N}(2V)/Z_N(V)^2$ $=4^N(N!)^2/(2N)!$; for two fixed distinguishable species it is $[Z_N(2V)/Z_N(V)]^2=4^N$. The first ratio exceeds one because $(2N)!/(N!)^2=\binom{2N}{N}<\sum_{j=0}^{2N}\binom{2N}{j}=4^N$. Under the final positional law, the $2N$ particles independently fall in either half with probability $1/2$, so the central binomial probability is $\binom{2N}{N}/4^N$, the reciprocal of the identical-particle ratio.

For each integer $n\ge1$, monotonicity of $\log x$ on unit intervals gives $$n\log n-n+1\le\log(n!)\le n\log n-n+1+\log n.$$ Indeed the lower bound integrates $\log x\le\log j$ on $[j-1,j]$ for $j=2,\ldots,n$, and the upper bound integrates $\log x\ge\log j$ on $[j,j+1]$ for $j=1,\ldots,n-1$, then adds $\log n$. Substitution for $n=N$ and $n=2N$ cancels the terms linear in $N$ in $N\log4+2\log(N!)-\log((2N)!)$, leaving a quantity bounded in absolute value by a constant multiple of $\log(N+1)$. Therefore $\Delta S_{\mathrm{identical}}/N\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.

boundaries.reason: The example assumes N>=1 in each compartment.

boundaries.evidence: N>=1 and T,m,a0>0 exclude a vacuum or zero-temperature normalization. Proof2.1 gives log(4^N(N!)^2/(2N)!)>0 at every finite N; proof3.1 makes it sublinear, not identically zero. The zero interaction U=0 is precisely the ideal model used in1.1.
Statement and proof review: Statement: The finite formula holds at N=1; the factorial and binomial expressions are defined.
Statement and proof review: Statement: The one-particle case is nondegenerate because both compartments have positive volume.
Statement and proof review: Statement: Both initial and final position volumes are finite and positive; no infinite-volume limit is used.

boundaries.reason: The finite combinatorial and Gaussian calculations use no choice principle.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof review: The exact entropy ratio is strictly positive for N>=1 by the strict central-binomial bound in the displayed step.

risk_review.notes: Checked all three verification steps and four suppliers. Gaussian scaling and integration by parts give finite energy; thus Gibbs entropy identity is used only in its valid finite-integrability scope, not its overstrong minimizer sentence. Counting ratios are exact for N>=1; central binomial coefficient is strictly smaller than 4^N, and positivity is retained. Monotone-log integral factorial bounds cancel the linear terms and give O(log(N+1)), including N=1. Bernoulli half-box probability refers to the symmetric labelled lift; the count event is invariant. Initial/final canonical preparations are stipulated ideal laws, no finite-data or dynamics assertion.

citations.quote:
For a fixed $N$, controls $\lambda$, measurable classical Hamiltonian
$H_{N,\lambda}:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, measurable for the
phase Borel sigma-algebra and taking energy values in joules, and the declared
physical reference measure $m_N^{\rm phys}$ of
[[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]], choose a prescribed
thermodynamic-temperature control $T>0$ in kelvins and
$\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$ using the SI temperature convention of
[[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$0<Z_N(\beta,\lambda):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H_{N,\lambda}}\,dm_N^{\rm phys}<\infty,$$
adopt the canonical state with density
$$\rho_{\beta,\lambda}=Z_N(\beta,\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\beta H_{N,\lambda}}$$
relative to $m_N^{\rm phys}$. Set $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Normalizability
is a required condition on the chosen model; bounded-below energy alone does
not imply it. This probability law is an adopted preparation, not a
consequence of deterministic mechanics or evidence of laboratory
equilibration.

Let $T>0$ be the prescribed temperature control in kelvins,
$\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and let the chemical-potential control $\mu$ have
units J per particle under the SI convention
[[def-td-si-quantities]]. In this adopted law, $\mu$ is the energy
coefficient conjugate to the dimensionless sector count $N$ in the weight
$e^{-\beta(H_N-\mu N)}$; no derivative with respect to integer $N$ is used.
For $N\ge1$, let $\Gamma_N$ and its reference
measure be those of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]], and let
$$H_N:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$$
be Borel measurable for the sector sigma-algebra
$\mathcal F_N$ generated by the open sets of $\Gamma_N$, with $+\infty$
marking forbidden states, and use the convention
$e^{-\beta(+\infty)}:=0$.
Define
the vacuum sector by $\Gamma_0=\{*\}$ with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\{*\}\}$, reference mass
$m_0^{\mathrm{phys}}(\{*\})=1$, particle number $N=0$, and vacuum Hamiltonian
$H_0(*)=0$. On the disjoint union $\mathcal G:=\bigsqcup_{N=0}^\infty\Gamma_N$,
use the sigma-algebra
$$\mathcal F_{\mathcal G}:=\{A\subseteq\mathcal G:A\cap\Gamma_N\in\mathcal F_N\text{ for every }N\ge0\},$$
where $\mathcal F_N$ is the declared measurable structure on sector $N$, and
the reference measure
$$m^{\mathrm{phys}}(A):=\sum_{N=0}^\infty m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(A\cap\Gamma_N).$$
This disjoint-union reference is sigma-finite because it is a countable sum
of the sigma-finite sector references, including the finite vacuum measure.
Let
$$\Xi(\beta,\mu):=\sum_{N=0}^\infty\int_{\Gamma_N} e^{-\beta(H_N-\mu N)}\,dm_N^{\rm phys}$$
satisfy $0<\Xi<\infty$. Adopt the probability measure on
$(\mathcal G,\mathcal F_{\mathcal G})$ with density
$$\rho(N,z):=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta(H_N(z)-\mu N)}$$
relative to $m^{\mathrm{phys}}$. The finiteness condition is
part of the model; it requires control of the sector sum and is not implied
by each finite-sector partition function being finite. Particle-exchange
preparation is an assumption, not a deduction from fixed-$N$ dynamics. Under
the vacuum convention above, the $N=0$ contribution to $\Xi$ is exactly one.

Fix integers $N,d\ge1$, a prescribed temperature control $T>0$ in kelvins,
$\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ as in [[def-td-si-quantities]], and external pressure
$P_{\rm ext}>0$ in J m$^{-d}$, a fixed dimensionless shape
$Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ that is Lebesgue measurable, meaning
$Q_1\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^d)$, and has Lebesgue measure
$|Q_1|_d:=\lambda_d(Q_1)=1$
([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
a positive volume reference $V_0$ in m$^d$. Write
$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)\in Q_1^N$, take $dy$ to be product Lebesgue measure on
$Q_1^N$, take $dp$ to be Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{dN}$, and take
$dV$ to be Lebesgue measure on $(0,\infty)$. Identify
the position domain at volume $V>0$ by $q_i=V^{1/d}y_i$. The Jacobian is
$V^N$, which is the full position-volume factor because $|Q_1|_d=1$. Adopt
the joint reference
$$d\nu_N=\frac{dV}{V_0}\,\frac{V^N\,dy\,dp}{N!a_0^{dN}},$$
where $a_0>0$ is the action reference in J s. The factors $dV/V_0$ and
$V^Ndy\,dp/a_0^{dN}$ are dimensionless. Let
$$H_N:(0,\infty)\times Q_1^N\times\mathbb R^{dN}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$$
be a product-measurable energy-valued Hamiltonian (in joules) for this
reference, with $+\infty$ marking forbidden states; set
$e^{-\beta(+\infty+P_{\rm ext}V)}:=0$. The product reference
$\nu_N$ is sigma-finite: $Q_1^N$ has finite measure, while $(0,\infty)$ and
$\mathbb R^{dN}$ have countable finite-measure exhaustions; the factor $V^N$
is finite on each set where $V$ is bounded. Assume
$$0<\Delta_N:=\int_0^\infty\!\int e^{-\beta(H_N(V,y,p)+P_{\rm ext}V)}\,d\nu_N<\infty.$$
Adopt the probability density
$$\rho_N(V,y,p):=\Delta_N^{-1}e^{-\beta(H_N(V,y,p)+P_{\rm ext}V)}$$
relative to $\nu_N$. The displayed
$N!$ is the single-species convention; for several indistinguishable species
with fixed counts $N_a$, replace it by $\prod_aN_a!$ as in
[[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. The factor $dV/V_0$ is an
explicit volume-reference convention; a different piston state measure gives
a different preparation. This postulate includes no piston kinetic energy
unless it is explicitly included in the Hamiltonian, and does not claim a
smooth wall dynamics.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
satisfies
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.

Let $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N,m_N)$ be a sigma-finite phase-reference measure
space from [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]; the cotangent construction uses
the stated Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]). A **statistical state** is a probability measure
$P$ on $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)$, meaning a countably additive measure with
$P(\Gamma_N)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). A **density** of $P$ relative to $m_N$ is a
measurable $\rho:\Gamma_N\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$P(A)=\int_A\rho\,dm_N\quad(A\in\mathcal F_N),\qquad \int_{\Gamma_N}\rho\,dm_N=1.$$
Equivalently, $P=\rho\,m_N$ in the definition of a measure with density
([[def-measure-with-density]]); integration against that density has the
meaning supplied by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]. A state need not
have a density.

An **observable** is a real-valued measurable function
$A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]).
Its expectation $\langle A\rangle_P:=\int A\,dP$ is used only when $A$ is
integrable, that is, $\int|A|\,dP<\infty$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). Its
variance is
$$\operatorname{Var}_P(A):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)^2\,dP$$
when $A^2$ is integrable. For square-integrable $A,B$, their covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_P(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)(B-\langle B\rangle_P)\,dP.$$
These expressions are finite under the stated square-integrability
hypotheses. Indeed, $P(\Gamma_N)=1$ makes $1\in L^2(P)$ with norm $1$.
By [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
$\int|A|\,dP\le(\int A^2\,dP)^{1/2}$, so the mean of a square-integrable
observable exists. If $a=\langle A\rangle_P$, then
$|A-a|^2\le2A^2+2a^2$ makes $A-a$ square-integrable; the same argument
applies to $B-b$. A second application of that inequality gives
$\int|(A-a)(B-b)|\,dP\le\|A-a\|_2\|B-b\|_2<\infty$.
Thus both the variance and covariance integrals above are well-defined.

If $P=\rho m_N$ and the integrals are defined, these expectations equal
$\int A\rho\,dm_N$ by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]].

A **macrostate map** is a measurable map
$M:(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)\to(Y,\mathcal G)$. Its induced state on $Y$ is
the pushforward $M_*P(B):=P(M^{-1}(B))$. The measure of a macrocell and an
entropy assigned to that macrostate are additional constructions; they are
not identical to the expectation or variance of a microscopic observable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a measure space and let $p,q$ be probability
densities relative to $m$, with $q>0$ almost everywhere on $\{p>0\}$. Define
the relative entropy
$$D(p\Vert q):=\int_{\{p>0\}}p\log(p/q)\,dm,$$
allowing $+\infty$. Then $D(p\Vert q)\ge0$, and equality holds exactly
when $p=q$ almost everywhere. For arbitrary probability densities, extend
$D(p\Vert q)$ to $+\infty$ if $\int_{\{q=0\}}p\,dm>0$.
In particular, let $H$ be extended-real measurable, finite $p$-almost
everywhere, let $\beta>0$, and suppose
$$0<Z=\int e^{-\beta H}dm<\infty,\quad q=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H},\quad \int p|H|dm<\infty,\quad \int|p\log p|dm<\infty.$$
For $S[p]:=-k\int p\log p\,dm$ and $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, with $k>0$
and $\beta kT=1$, one has
$$D(p\Vert q)=\beta\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-F-TS[p]\bigr)\ge0.$$
Write $\mathcal A$ for the probability densities satisfying these finite
energy and absolute entropy conditions. For every measurable $H$ with the
stated positive finite $Z$, define the **extended relative free energy** on
all probability densities by
$$\mathcal F_{\rm ext}[p]:=F+\beta^{-1}D(p\Vert q)\in[F,+\infty].$$
It agrees with $\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]$ on $\mathcal A$ and has the
unique minimizer $q$, up to almost-everywhere equality, even when the
separate energy and entropy integrals of $q$ are not finite. Moreover,
$$\inf_{p\in\mathcal A}\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]\bigr)=F.$$
This infimum is attained if and only if
$\int q|H|dm<\infty$ and $\int|q\log q|dm<\infty$; in that case its
unique minimizer is $q$. Otherwise no density in $\mathcal A$ attains the
infimum. Products with a zero density are taken as zero on the forbidden
set, and densities may be redefined on null sets. These mathematical
claims do not derive a physical preparation.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: For a canonical density $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$, $\log\rho=-\beta H-\log Z$. Integrating against $\rho$ gives $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$, so $-k_BT\log Z=U-TS$ because $k_BT\beta=1$. For any competitor $p$, [F3] gives $D(p\Vert\rho)=\beta(\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]-F)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p=\rho$ almost everywhere. At fixed model, $U=-\partial_\beta\log Z$ by [F2]. Differentiating $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ and using $d\beta/dT=-1/(k_BT^2)$ gives $\partial_TF=-S$, proving the canonical differential.

On the grand disjoint union, $\log\rho=-\beta(H-\mu N)-\log\Xi$. Integration gives $S=k_B(\log\Xi+\beta(U-\mu\bar N))$, hence $\Omega=-k_BT\log\Xi=U-TS-\mu\bar N$. Applying [F2] to the sufficient statistics $H$ and $N$ gives $\partial_\mu\log\Xi=\beta\bar N$ and $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi|_\mu=U-\mu\bar N$. Thus $\partial_\mu\Omega=-\bar N$ and $\partial_T\Omega=-S$, proving the grand differential at fixed model.

For the joint isothermal-isobaric density, $\log\rho=-\beta(H+P_{\rm ext}V)-\log\Delta$. Integration gives $S=k_B(\log\Delta+\beta\langle H+P_{\rm ext}V\rangle)$ and therefore the displayed $G_{\rm isoP}$. Applying [F2] to $B=H+P_{\rm ext}V$ gives $-\partial_\beta\log\Delta|_P=\langle B\rangle$, while $\partial_P\log\Delta=-\beta\langle V\rangle$; hence $\partial_TG_{\rm isoP}=-S$ and $\partial_PG_{\rm isoP}=\langle V\rangle$. This proves the stated differential and completes the conditional identities.
